transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Um, well, I guess what finally made me come in today is... well, I recently finished my bachelor's degree, so I'm supposed to be entering the real world and starting my career now, right? But honestly, I am just completely failing at being a functioning adult. I keep forgetting the most basic, everyday things. 

And I don't mean just misplacing my keys every now and then, I mean I am constantly forgetting to pay my bills. I'll literally have the money sitting right there in my checking account, but I just... don't do it. The thought to actually log in and pay it just evaporates from my mind until I get a massive late fee or a shut-off notice in the mail. And errands are the same way—I'll leave the house with a whole plan in my head to go to the post office and drop off a package and then go to the pharmacy, and I'll somehow just completely forget and come home having done absolutely none of it. Showing up for appointments is a whole other nightmare, too. I actually had to set, like, four different alarms on my phone just to make sure I didn't forget to come to this exact appointment today. 

But I think the real breaking point, the thing that really made me realize I need to talk to a doctor, is that this is starting to cost me real, actual opportunities in my life. Since I don't have a job right now, I've been applying everywhere, but when recruiters actually email me back to set up an interview, I'll look at the email on my phone, tell myself, "Okay, I need to write a really professional reply to this as soon as I sit down at my laptop," and then it just completely ceases to exist in my brain. By the time I remember, like, a week later, the interview slots are all gone or the position is filled. It's just so incredibly frustrating because I know I need to do these things, I want to do them, but my brain just drops them entirely and I don't know how to stop doing it.
Have you struggled with these types of issues—like forgetfulness, losing things, or difficulty completing tasks—since you were a child, or is this something that only started recently?

Oh, wow, um, no, this is definitely not new at all. I mean, it feels a lot worse now because the consequences are bigger, like jobs and bills and stuff, but if I really think back... gosh, it’s been happening for as long as I can remember. Like, literally going all the way back to elementary school. 

I actually found a box of my old report cards recently when I was moving out of my dorm, and it was kind of a wake-up call, honestly. Every single year, my teachers would write basically the exact same paragraph in the comments section. They’d always start by saying I was "bright" or "had so much potential," which, you know, sounds nice, but then the rest of it was just a laundry list of everything I was doing wrong. They’d say I was constantly losing my worksheets, which was true—I would do the homework, put it in my backpack, and then it would just vanish into another dimension. Or they’d say I rushed through directions without reading them, which I still do, honestly. I’d just glance at the first sentence and start working, and then realize halfway through that I was doing the wrong thing. 

And it wasn't just the forgetfulness, either. The comments always mentioned that I talked out of turn constantly. I just could not stop myself from blurting things out if a thought popped into my head. It felt like if I didn't say it right then, I would explode, or I'd forget it completely. And my desk... oh my gosh, my desk was a disaster zone. My third-grade teacher actually made me stay inside during recess once just to clean it out because I had shoved so many crumpled up papers and half-eaten snacks and broken pencils in there that I couldn't even find the assignments she was trying to collect. So yeah, I guess I've always been like this. It's just that when you're eight, your mom or your teacher eventually steps in and fixes it for you, but now that I'm twenty-two, there's nobody to do that, and I'm just kind of drowning in it.
In your daily life now as an adult, do you still find yourself feeling restless, or do you find that you still frequently interrupt others or blurt out answers before someone has finished speaking?

Oh, definitely. Yes. The blurting things out is still a huge, huge problem for me. It's actually one of the things I'm most embarrassed about, especially now that I'm trying to be, you know, a professional adult. It's like my brain is running on a completely different speed than everyone else's, and I just can't put the brakes on my mouth. 

I'll be in a conversation—and this happens all the time, not just with friends, but even in the few interviews I *have* managed to actually show up for—and the other person will start asking a question or explaining something, and the second I think I know where they're going with it, I just jump right in. I literally cannot wait for them to finish their sentence. It's like this physical pressure builds up in my chest, and if I don't get the thought out immediately, it's going to disappear forever, or I'm just going to burst. 

So I'll cut them off, and I'll start talking, and then... it's a disaster. Half the time, I realize mid-sentence that I completely misinterpreted what they were going to ask, so I end up answering the wrong question entirely. Or, I'll see the look on their face—that sort of polite but annoyed look where they're clearly thinking, "Wow, she just totally talked over me"—and I feel so incredibly stupid. I'll sit there thinking, "Why did you do that? Why couldn't you just wait two more seconds for them to finish?" But in the moment, it just slips out before I can even process that I'm doing it. 

It happened just last week, actually, when I was talking to a recruiter on the phone. She was asking me about my coursework, and she started saying, "So, I see you took a class in..." and before she could even say the name of the class, I just yelled out, "Yes, data analysis, and I loved it, and here's a project I did!" And she just paused and said, "...I was going to ask about your communications seminar." I wanted the ground to swallow me whole. It's just so frustrating because I know it makes me look rude or like I'm not listening, but I *am* listening! I'm just... listening too fast, I guess? I don't know. But yes, I definitely still do that all the time.
